section: Sources › [S-S] Lander JA, Weltman BJ, So SS — Limits (just above 'Calculations withdrawn and remaining limits')
sentence_as_it_stands: The withdrawal is administrative rather than a finding of error, and the 2006 analysis stands as published, but it is no longer a current Cochrane review and nothing has replaced it.
quote: Presently, this pairwise meta-analysis of 10 studies pooling over 890 pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia with EMLA cream or amethocaine gel is the first and most comprehensive review on the topic.
corrected_wording: The withdrawal is administrative rather than a finding of error, and the 2006 analysis stands as published, but it is no longer a current Cochrane review. Later meta-analyses of the same comparison in children exist: Pywell 2015 (3 randomised trials; first-time cannulation success, no significant difference; PMID 25351196) and Varghese 2024 (10 studies; amethocaine favoured on child-reported absence of pain in the 5 studies reporting it, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41–0.82, with no significant difference on child- or parent-reported VAS, observed pain score or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia; PMID 38429571).
notes: Same sentence as claim D068 (refuted; own-question and extra-study updates in this part); recorded for its page location and version. No ranking rests on this source note. Varghese 2024 does not cite the Lander review and calls itself the first review on the topic, which is inaccurate (Lander 2006; Taddio 2002, which it cites). Its first-attempt cannulation result (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99, 3 trials) is left out of the corrected wording because none of the three trials was significant on its own and the narrow interval follows the Hartung-Knapp method (ordinary pooling of the plotted estimates gives 0.89–1.09).

sentence_as_it_stands: What it costs the claim is currency, not validity: the estimates are frozen at a 2006 search, **Cochrane no longer stands behind them as up to date**, and nothing has replaced the review on that exact head-to-head \[S182\]. **The comparison is carried instead by an independent replication that is current**: a network meta-analysis of **40 randomised trials in 4,481 children** ranked amethocaine first of nine methods with a probability of **57.6%** \[S182\].
quote: Presently, this pairwise meta-analysis of 10 studies pooling over 890 pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia with EMLA cream or amethocaine gel is the first and most comprehensive review on the topic.
corrected_wording: What it costs the claim is currency, not validity: the estimates are frozen at a 2006 search and Cochrane no longer stands behind them as up to date. Two later pairwise meta-analyses address the same head-to-head in children: Pywell 2015 (3 randomised trials; first-time cannulation success RR 1.046, CI 0.975–1.122, not significant; PMID 25351196) and Varghese 2024 (10 studies; amethocaine favoured on child-reported absence of pain in 5 studies, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41–0.82, with no significant difference on child- or parent-reported VAS, observed pain score or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia; PMID 38429571). A 2025 network meta-analysis of 40 randomised trials in 4,481 children ranked amethocaine first of nine methods with a probability of 57.6% [S182].
notes: Second place the D068 error appears, here in the Reference, where the next paragraph's prilocaine-free option leans on the comparison (finding F03). The S182 register entry does not repeat the error ('any trial after the 2006 search is outside it'). Pywell's figures are from its abstract (PMID 25351196, cached), cited by Varghese as ref 26. Varghese's first-attempt cannulation estimate is left out for the reason given in F01.

sentence_as_it_stands: **That reopens a prilocaine-free option this reference closes elsewhere.** The pre-capsaicin anaesthetic in §4.2.4 is the one place a prilocaine-containing product is accepted for want of an alternative, and amethocaine [dose figure omitted] is an alternative that beat that product in a Cochrane review whose analysis stands and whose currency does not, and again in a 2025 network meta-analysis that is current.
quote: Compared to amethocaine gel, EMLA cream was associated with lower rates of child-reported absence of pain (RR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.82; p = 0.011). … There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported VAS (SMD, 0.43; 95% CI, −1.46 to 2.31; p = 0.525).
corrected_wording: The pre-capsaicin anaesthetic in §4.2.4 is the one place a prilocaine-containing product is accepted for want of an alternative. Amethocaine is prilocaine-free; in children's needle procedures it reduced pain against that product in a Cochrane review whose analysis stands and whose currency does not, and it was ranked first of nine methods in a 2025 network meta-analysis, while a 2024 pairwise meta-analysis (Varghese, 10 studies) found it ahead on child-reported absence of pain (5 studies, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41–0.82) but not on child- or parent-reported VAS, observed pain score or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 3 trials found no significant difference in first-time cannulation success. None of these studies tested anaesthesia before a capsaicin patch.
notes: A recommendation resting on EMLA-versus-amethocaine evidence (the brief's candidate for ranking-reweigh). Accurate about the Cochrane review, but it leaves out the two current pairwise syntheses, whose results are mixed by outcome. Varghese's first-attempt cannulation estimate (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99, 3 trials) is not used as support because none of the three trials was significant on its own and the narrow interval follows the Hartung-Knapp method (ordinary pooling of the plotted estimates: 0.89–1.09). Varghese also summarises Taddio 2002 (8 studies): equally effective when used according to instructions, tetracaine better at equal application times; the Cochrane review's per-instructions sensitivity analysis (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46–0.89) favoured amethocaine, so these reviews do not settle the application-time question. One of Varghese's pooled studies (McCafferty 1997) is a laser study in patients over 12.

sentence_as_it_stands: **That Cochrane review was withdrawn on 23 May 2013**, because its authors were no longer available to complete an update; the notice alleges no error, so the analysis stands and only its currency does not, and the network meta-analysis is the current replication of the same comparison. **That reopens the pre-Qutenza question**: amethocaine [dose figure omitted] is a prilocaine-free alternative that beat the lidocaine-prilocaine cream in a Cochrane review that is withdrawn but unretracted, and again in a network meta-analysis that is current.
quote: Compared to amethocaine gel, EMLA cream was associated with lower rates of child-reported absence of pain (RR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.82; p = 0.011). … There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported VAS (SMD, 0.43; 95% CI, −1.46 to 2.31; p = 0.525).
corrected_wording: That Cochrane review was withdrawn on 23 May 2013, because its authors were no longer available to complete an update; the notice alleges no error, so the analysis stands and only its currency does not. Later syntheses of the same comparison in children differ by outcome: a 2025 network meta-analysis ranked amethocaine first of nine methods; a 2024 pairwise meta-analysis (Varghese, 10 studies) found it ahead on child-reported absence of pain (5 studies, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41–0.82) but not on child- or parent-reported VAS, observed pain score or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 3 trials found no significant difference in first-time cannulation success. Amethocaine is prilocaine-free; none of these studies tested it before a capsaicin patch.
notes: 'the network meta-analysis is the current replication of the same comparison' leaves out the two pairwise meta-analyses (Pywell 2015, Varghese 2024). The same sentences, followed by the line that amethocaine is the best-supported option before a capsaicin patch, also stand on the page titled 'Duplicate or Superceded - DELETE ME — 3 — Product Guide, Plain English' (https://app.notion.com/p/3d410b7903aa81ac9233cb71f5e5b038, as of 2026-10-01T03:54:25.660Z); not recorded separately because that page is marked for deletion. Varghese's first-attempt cannulation estimate (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99, 3 trials) is not used as support because none of the three trials was significant on its own and the narrow interval follows the Hartung-Knapp method (ordinary pooling of the plotted estimates: 0.89–1.09). Varghese also summarises Taddio 2002 (8 studies): equally effective when used according to instructions, tetracaine better at equal application times; the Cochrane review's per-instructions sensitivity analysis (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46–0.89) favoured amethocaine, so these reviews do not settle the application-time question. One of Varghese's pooled studies (McCafferty 1997) is a laser study in patients over 12.

section: Ranks 19 to 23 · On the list, and not to buy › 19 · EMLA cream
sentence_as_it_stands: Ask the clinic what it uses and whether it cools, buy nothing before that answer, and where it wants a cream, ask about **amethocaine [dose figure omitted]**, which is prilocaine-free and beat this one in a Cochrane review — a review Cochrane **withdrew on 23 May 2013** because its authors could not complete an update, alleging no error in it, and whose result a current network meta-analysis of **40 trials in 4,481 children** reproduces.
quote: Compared to amethocaine gel, EMLA cream was associated with lower rates of child-reported absence of pain (RR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.82; p = 0.011). … There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported VAS (SMD, 0.43; 95% CI, −1.46 to 2.31; p = 0.525).
corrected_wording: Amethocaine is prilocaine-free. In children's needle procedures it beat this cream on pain in a Cochrane review that Cochrane withdrew on 23 May 2013 because its authors could not complete an update, alleging no error in it; a 2025 network meta-analysis of 40 trials in 4,481 children ranked it first of nine methods; a 2024 pairwise meta-analysis (Varghese, 10 studies) found it ahead on child-reported absence of pain (5 studies, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41–0.82) but not on child- or parent-reported VAS, observed pain score or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 3 trials found no significant difference in first-time cannulation success. None of these studies tested anaesthesia before a capsaicin patch.
notes: The rank-19 entry's pointer to amethocaine rests on the EMLA-versus-amethocaine comparison, and 'whose result a current network meta-analysis ... reproduces' leaves out the two pairwise syntheses and their mixed results. The corrected wording covers the evidence clause only; the entry's advice clauses are left to the record's owner. EMLA's rank itself rests on its neuropathic evidence, not on this comparison. Varghese's first-attempt cannulation estimate (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99, 3 trials) is not used as support because none of the three trials was significant on its own and the narrow interval follows the Hartung-Knapp method (ordinary pooling of the plotted estimates: 0.89–1.09). Varghese also summarises Taddio 2002 (8 studies): equally effective when used according to instructions, tetracaine better at equal application times; the Cochrane review's per-instructions sensitivity analysis (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46–0.89) favoured amethocaine, so these reviews do not settle the application-time question. One of Varghese's pooled studies (McCafferty 1997) is a laser study in patients over 12.
